t.7.20.1: Then the lord of the Rākṣasas, terrifying mortals across the earth, came upon Nārada, the foremost of sages, within that cloud.
t.7.20.2: But Nārada, the divine sage of great splendor and boundless radiance, standing upon the back of a cloud, spoke to Rāvaṇa, who was seated in the Puṣpaka.
t.7.20.3: O lord of the rākṣasas, gentle one, stay, O son of Viśravas! O you of noble lineage, I am pleased by your mighty exploits.
t.7.20.4: I have indeed been greatly gratified by Viṣṇu through his slayings of the Daityas, by Tārkṣya's assaults upon the serpents, and by you through your crushing of foes in battle.
t.7.20.5: I shall tell you something worth hearing, if you will listen; and having heard it, you must act on it at once, O bull among Rākṣasas.
t.7.20.6: Why is this world being slain by you, who cannot be slain by the gods? For this world is already slain, since it has passed under the sway of Death.
t.7.20.7: Behold, O mighty-armed lord of the rākṣasas, this human world of manifold and wondrous affairs, whose course cannot be known.
t.7.20.8: In some places music and dances are enjoyed by joyful people, while elsewhere others, stricken with grief, weep, their eyes and faces streaming with torrents of tears.
t.7.20.9: Mother, affection for father and son, wife, and delightful kinsmen: by these and by delusion this man is ruined, and he does not perceive his own suffering.
t.7.20.11: Thus addressed, the lord of Laṅkā, as if blazing with his own energy, laughed aloud, saluted Nārada, and then spoke to him there.
t.7.20.10: So what is gained by tormenting in this way a world already undone by delusion? The world of mortals has already been conquered by you, gentle one; there is no doubt.
t.7.20.12: O great sage, you who roam among the gods and Gandharvas and who delight in battle, I am indeed resolved to go to Rasātala, seeking victory.
t.7.20.13: Then, having conquered the three worlds and brought the Nāgas and the gods under my control, I shall indeed churn the ocean, the abode of liquids, for the sake of the nectar of immortality.
t.7.20.14: Then the blessed seer Nārada said to Daśagrīva: "Where, now, will you be going by this road?"
t.7.20.15: This path, O tormentor of foes, very hard to travel and hard to assail, indeed leads toward the city of Yama, the king of the Pitṛs.
t.7.20.17: Therefore, O great brahmin, I, intent on slaying Vaivasvata, go to the southern quarter, where dwells the king, the son of Sūrya.
t.7.20.16: Daśānana, letting out a laugh as bright as an autumn cloud, said, "So be it," and then spoke these words.
t.7.20.18: For, O blessed one, I, eager for battle, have vowed in my wrath, O lord: "I shall conquer the four guardians of the worlds."
t.7.20.19: Therefore I have set out for the city of the king of the ancestors; I shall unite with death him who causes torment to living beings.
t.7.20.20: Having spoken thus and saluted that sage, Daśagrīva set out toward the southern quarter together with his delighted ministers.
t.7.20.21: But Nārada of great splendour, the foremost of brahmins, resorting to meditation for a moment, reflected, shining like a smokeless fire.
t.7.20.22: How can that Kāla be slain, by whom the three worlds, together with Indra and with all beings moving and unmoving, are afflicted when their lifespan and dharma are exhausted?
t.7.20.23: How is it that this lord of the Rākṣasas goes of his own accord to him from whom the three worlds constantly flee, stricken with fear?
t.7.20.24: He who is both the ordainer and the sustainer, dealing with good and evil deeds as they deserve, he by whom the three worlds have been conquered, how indeed will one conquer him?
t.7.20.25: Having acted thus, what further arrangement will he now make? Filled with curiosity, I shall go to the abode of Yama.
